flawed_step: Step 4: the claim that the MST is unique, so both outputs must be the same edge set. This only holds when edge weights are distinct. Tie-breaking is unspecified, so it can fail.
counterexample: Triangle on vertices a, b, c with w(ab)=w(bc)=w(ca)=1. Kruskal, sorting edges as ab, bc, ca: it adds ab, adds bc, then rejects ca because it would close a cycle. Output {ab, bc}. Prim starting at a, breaking the tie among ab and ac in favour of ac: it adds ac. The cut edges are then ab and cb, both weight 1; it picks ab. Output {ac, ab}. Both trees have weight 2, the minimum, so both are MSTs, but they are different edge sets.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt:
1. Kruskal's output is a minimum spanning tree (MST), whatever the tie-breaking. JUSTIFIED: this is the standard cut/cycle-property correctness proof and does not depend on tie-breaks.
2. Prim's output is an MST, whatever the start vertex and tie-breaking. JUSTIFIED: standard cut-property argument.
3. So both outputs are spanning trees of minimum total weight. JUSTIFIED: follows from steps 1 and 2.
4. The MST of a connected weighted graph is unique, so the two outputs are the same edge set. NOT JUSTIFIED: uniqueness is only guaranteed when edge weights are distinct (more precisely, when no ties cause ambiguity). The definitions allow equal weights and arbitrary tie-breaks. Example: in a triangle with all weights 1, each of the three 2-edge trees is an MST.
5. So every legal Kruskal run and every legal Prim run give the same edge set. NOT JUSTIFIED: it depends entirely on step 4. It is also false: in the triangle above, Kruskal with order ab, bc, ca outputs {ab, bc}, while Prim from a (tie broken toward ac, then ab) outputs {ac, ab}. Both are legal runs with MST outputs of weight 2, but the edge sets differ.
Conclusion: steps 1–3 hold, but the argument breaks at step 4, and the counterexample shows the statement is false as defined. It would only be true under extra assumptions, such as distinct weights or a shared consistent tie-breaking order.
